title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling playbook, benchmarks and runbooks
author: Asha Patel
body:
Summary

This document consolidates the serving runtime team canonical references for runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, recent release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is the single-source guide for on-call engineers, performance owners, and platform product managers who operate or evolve the inference runtime.

Scope

- Runtime architecture: high-level components and data flow.
- Kernel scheduling: design rationale and tunables for the token/kernel scheduler.
- Profiling playbook: step-by-step instructions and example commands to collect perf traces.
- Benchmarking suite: test harness, scenarios, regression thresholds, and output interpretation.
- Release notes: summary of changes to scheduling and kernels (last 3 releases).
- Known issues & runbooks: tracked production incidents and troubleshooting steps.

Owners & Contacts

- Primary owner: Runtime Team (engineering)
- Primary author: Asha Patel (engineer, runtime)
- On-call rotation: runtime-sre@redwood.internal
- Performance lead: Liam Chen
- Release coordinator: Priya Nair

Architecture overview

The serving runtime is a horizontally scalable GPU-optimized inference engine composed of:

1) Front-door router (redwood-router)
- Handles authentication, tenant routing, and model variant selection.
- Routes requests to pools based on policy (latency SLO, cost tier, region).

2) Worker agents (redwood-worker)
- Hosts the inference execution: model weights, KV cache, tokenizer, and kernel runtime.
- Exposes a local gRPC API used by the router.

3) Token/kernel scheduler (redwood-scheduler)
- Implements batching, kernel selection, and preemption priorities.
- Central to balancing throughput and latency SLOs.

4) KV/Prefix cache (redwood-cache)
- Shared across worker replicas per-tenant where allowed; reduces repeated computation for common prefixes.

5) Observability & Telemetry
- Metrics: per-request latency (p50/p95/p99), tokens/sec, batch size distribution, GPU utilization, memory headroom.
- Traces: request lifecycle tracing from router -> scheduler -> worker.

Component interactions

- Router assigns requests to worker pools and attaches scheduling hints (priority, max-latency).
- Scheduler aggregates compatible requests into batches and selects kernels based on sequence length and quantization profile.
- Worker executes kernels and streams tokens back to the router.
- Cache is consulted before scheduling to short-circuit generation for cached prefixes.

Kernel scheduling: design and policies

Goals
- Meet latency SLOs (p99) for interactive workloads while maximizing GPU throughput.
- Minimize tail-latency amplification due to straggler batches or long sequences.

Key concepts

- Dynamic batching: group requests across tenants (respecting isolation policies) up to batch_size_max or max_wait_ms.
- Token-aware scheduling: prefer batching requests with similar sequence lengths to reduce padding overhead.
- Preemption and priority: can preempt lower-priority batches for high-priority/low-latency requests.
- Kernel selection: choose between optimized attention kernels, grouped GEMM kernels, and quantized kernels based on model and hardware capability.

Important tunables (global config)

| parameter                | description                                         | typical value |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|---------------|
| batch_size_max          | maximum batch size for a single kernel invocation   | "32"          |
| batch_timeout_ms        | max time to wait to form a batch                    | "6"           |
| token_grouping_window   | ms window for grouping by token length              | "3"           |
| preemption_enabled      | allow preempt lower priority batches                | "true"        |
| kernel_profile          | kernel selection policy (latency/cost/throughput)   | "latency"     |
| quantized_kernels       | use int8/4 kernels when available                   | "true"        |

Note: values above are defaults; per-model profiles override when specified.

Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

When to run profiling
- New model onboarding (first 1M tokens of traffic).
- Regression investigation after perf alert (>10% p99 increase).
- Before changing kernel selection or global scheduling tunables.

Preparation
1. Identify target worker(s) and model version.
2. Ensure nsys and metrics exporter are installed on the host (runtime images include nsys v2024.2+).
3. Reserve a staging GPU pool or use canary lane to avoid production noise.

Profiling steps

1) Collect a system-level trace (nsys):
```
nsys profile -o /tmp/runtrace -t cuda,osrt --capture-range=nvtx --duration=60 --force-overwrite --trace-fork-before-exec true --sample=none /usr/local/bin/redwood-worker --model <MODEL> --port <PORT>
```
2) Aggregate runtime metrics alongside the trace (Prometheus scrape or local exporter):
- Collect GPU utilization, SM efficiency, memory footprint, kernel launch count.

3) Run a micro-benchmark to isolate kernel performance (on the worker):
```
/usr/local/bin/runtime-microbench --model <MODEL> --seq-len 128 --batch-sizes 1,2,4,8,16 --quant_modes int8,float16
```
4) Capture KV cache hit/miss distribution and batch size histogram (use /metrics endpoint):
```
curl -s http://localhost:9100/metrics | grep "kv_cache" -A 5
```
5) Post-process traces: generate flamegraph and identify >50ms kernel launches that account for p99 pressure.

What to collect
- nsys trace (.qdrep/.nsys-rep)
- batch_size_histogram (last 6 minutes)
- per-kernel latency distribution (from trace)
- GPU SM efficiency and occupancy
- KV cache hit rate

Interpreting results
- High padding overhead: many small-length requests batched with long ones -> increase token_grouping_window or split by sequence-length lanes.
- Low SM utilization with large batches: kernel choice mismatch (try grouped GEMM or fused kernels).
- Frequent small kernel launches with low occupancy: consider kernel fusion or increase batch_timeout_ms slightly.

Benchmarking suite

Overview
- The benchmarking suite (redwood-bench) is a deterministic load generator used for regression testing and capacity planning. It supports: latency-focused traces, throughput streams, and synthetic prompt mixes.

Core scenarios
- interactive-short: seq_len=64, target p95 latency < 120ms
- interactive-medium: seq_len=256, target p95 latency < 250ms
- batch-throughput: mixed seq_len, sustained tokens/sec target for each GPU
- embedding-latency: single request embedding latency targets

Example config (bench-config.yaml):
```
scenarios:
  - name: interactive-short
    qps: 50
    seq_len: 64
    concurrency: 8
    duration_s: 300
  - name: batch-throughput
    qps: 200
    seq_len: [64,128,256]
    concurrency: 64
    duration_s: 600
```

Regression thresholds
- p95 latency increase > 10% or p99 increase > 5% compared to golden baseline triggers a performance regression ticket.
- Token/sec drop > 8% at same configuration triggers capacity re-evaluation.

Interpreting outputs
- The bench output JSON contains: timestamps, p50/p95/p99 latencies, tokens_per_sec, batch_size_distribution, max_gpu_mem_mb.
- Compare against baseline with the provided compare script:
```
redwood-bench-compare --baseline baseline-2026-03-01.json --candidate run-2026-03-25.json --output report.html
```

Release notes (recent changes)

- 2026-03-20: kernel selection update: enabled fused attention kernel on A100 and H100 where model seq_len <= 512; default kernel_profile set to latency.
- 2026-02-14: scheduler preemption bug fix: resolved race when canceling low-priority batches leading to temporary batch starvation.
- 2026-01-10: quantized_kernels: enabled faster INT8 matmul for compatible models; measured avg 1.7x throughput improvement for embeddings.

Known issues & workarounds

1) Issue: Occasional p99 spikes when mixed very short and very long sequence requests are processed in the same worker pool.
Workaround: Create separate lanes for short and long sequences using router policy 'sequence_length_bucket'. Permanent fix: we are rolling out token-aware scheduler lanes (ETA: 2026-04-10).

2) Issue: nsys traces on some host kernels show missing kernel names when using older CUDA drivers (pre-11.8).
Workaround: Upgrade driver to 11.8+ on staging/prod GPUs.

3) Issue: Cache invalidation race during model rollout occasionally returns stale KV entries for 30s.
Workaround: Use rollout strategy 'drain-then-swap' when enabling new model weights for tenant-sensitive deployments.

Runtime runbooks (triage & recovery)

Severe p99 latency regression (page P0)
1. Pager receives alert from pagerduty; on-call acknowledges.
2. Run quick health checks:
   - curl router /healthz and worker /healthz
   - check Prometheus: p99 latency, batch_size_distribution, GPU util, queue_length
3. If GPU saturation observed (gpu_util > 92%), scale up canary pool or enable burst capacity (ops runbook: scale-gpu-pool).
4. If high padding overhead (many small requests with one large request), create temporary routing rule to separate long-running requests: route sequence_length > 512 -> low-priority pool.
5. Collect nsys trace for 60s on an affected worker (see profiling steps).
6. If regression matches kernel change in last release, perform rollback: set kernel_profile to previous value and trigger config rollout.
7. Post-incident: file incident review and associate perf traces and bench comparisons.

Worker OOM during large rollout
1. Detect via node-exporter OOM counters and worker crashloop.
2. Temporarily disable new rollout and roll back to previous model.
3. Increase per-worker memory headroom or reduce max_concurrent_requests in router policy.
4. Schedule follow-up: increase worker RAM or split model across more replicas.

Team wiki & onboarding notes

- All new runtime hires should complete the 1-week onboarding checklist in the runtime team wiki. Key pages: profiling basics, bench-runbook, scheduler-primer.
- Development guidelines: open an ADR for any change that alters default scheduling tunables or kernel selection heuristics.
- Weekly cadence: performance review in the weekly runtime sync (Tues 10:00) with a rotating 'perf owner' reporting benchmark comparisons.

Appendix: common configs

Default per-model profile (YAML snippet):
```
model_profiles:
  - model: redwood-open-7b
    batch_size_max: 24
    batch_timeout_ms: 5
    kernel_profile: latency
    quantized_kernels: true
```

Contact matrix and escalation
- Pager (P0/P1): runtime on-call -> runtime-sre -> infra-sre -> platform eng.
- Performance regressions (non-urgent): assign to performance lead (Liam Chen) and open a PR with proposed kernel/scheduler changes and bench results.
